questions.question: What does empirical evaluation do in interactive system development?
options: It evaluates the usability of a developed system with end users.
It gathers the functional requirements before design.
It specifies the work context for the system.
It tests code until the system is executable.
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation is the stage in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.

questions.question: Which stage does empirical evaluation follow in interactive system development?
options: The requirement-gathering stage.
The code testing stage.
The system-design stage.
The optimization stage.
questions.explanation: In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage.

questions.question: Why does code testing not prove that an interactive system is usable?
options: It produces an executable system but does not establish usability.
It compares interface speed by measuring characters per minute.
It only evaluates a limited prototype rather than the end system.
It depends mainly on users' subjective quality judgments.
questions.explanation: Code testing produces an executable system, but it does not establish that the system is usable.

questions.question: Why can quick prototype evaluations not provide a conclusive usability assessment?
options: They evaluate the fully implemented system, so their results are too late to judge the overall usability of the end system.
They collect behavioral data in a controlled experiment, so their results are too formal to judge the overall usability of the end system.
They are limited-scale evaluations, so their results are too limited to judge the overall usability of the end system.
They use a large number of evaluators, so their results are too broad to judge the overall usability of the end system.
questions.explanation: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can identify major issues but cannot give a conclusive result about overall end-system usability.

questions.question: What is required for a conclusive usability assessment of an overall system?
options: Evaluating a limited prototype, preferably with a smaller number of users, through a quick early check.
Collecting subjective quality opinions from a small group of users.
Comparing the system with a familiar application by asking users which one is better.
Evaluating the fully implemented system, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.
questions.explanation: A conclusive usability assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with more users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

questions.question: What type of research is a controlled experiment used for usability evaluation?
options: A code testing stage
A requirement-gathering stage
Empirical research
A quick prototype evaluation
questions.explanation: A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

questions.question: What is a quick prototype evaluation?
options: A code testing stage that produces an executable system but does not establish usability.
A limited-scale early evaluation that uses a limited number of evaluators on prototypes.
A controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data from the fully implemented system.
A large-scale final evaluation that uses many evaluators on the fully implemented system.
questions.explanation: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the four stages of an empirical or usability study?
options: Formulate research questions, determine variables, design and execute the experiment, and analyze the data.
Gather requirements, design the system, implement the code, and test the executable.
Choose a user group, run the virtual tour, collect subjective opinions, and compare with MS Word.
Evaluate a prototype, test the code, optimize resources, and deploy the system.
questions.explanation: An empirical study moves from research questions to variable determination, then to experiment design and execution, and finally to objective data analysis.

questions.question: Why are variables determined after the research questions in an empirical study?
options: Because subjective user feedback cannot be collected without them.
Because a controlled experiment cannot be designed or executed without them.
Because an executable system cannot be produced without them.
Because a quick prototype evaluation cannot identify major usability issues without them.
questions.explanation: Determining variables follows the research questions; without those variables, a controlled experiment cannot be designed or executed.

activities.title: Order the stages of an empirical usability study

items.title: Order the stages of an empirical usability study
steps: Design and execute an experiment to collect data
Analyze data to reach a reliable conclusion

questions.question: Which activity describes an empirical study after a system has been fully implemented?
options: Choosing user groups such as pilgrims, students, or tourists
Building and evaluating a quick prototype to find major usability issues
Setting up and executing an experiment to collect empirical data for usability analysis
Writing functional requirements before the system is designed
questions.explanation: An empirical study after full implementation involves setting up an experiment, executing it, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure usability.

questions.question: What is the first stage in an empirical study?
options: Executing the data collection
Determining the experimental variables
Analyzing the empirical data
Formulating a research question
questions.explanation: The first stage is formulating the research question, and later observations, data collection, and analysis are based on that question.

questions.question: Why is the research question "Is the new text entry GUI good?" considered problematic?
options: Because it produces an objective speed measurement in characters per minute
Because user judgments may be divided, so no clear conclusion can be drawn
Because it compares the new interface directly with Microsoft Word
Because it can be settled by evaluating a quick prototype
questions.explanation: Asking several users to judge whether the GUI is good can produce split judgments, making an answer and conclusion unlikely.

questions.question: Why does asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word not provide a definitive quality conclusion?
options: Because it asks users to complete a timed text-entry task.
Because it can be decided by comparing characters per minute.
Because 'better' has the same meaning for every user.
Because 'better' can mean more or fewer features depending on the user.
questions.explanation: A 'better' question does not give a definitive quality conclusion because different users may mean more or fewer features by 'better'.

questions.question: Why is a question about entering text faster than Microsoft Word less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question?
options: Because it lets each user choose any text and typing goal.
Because it asks users to rate the overall quality of the interface.
Because it removes the need to collect user feedback.
Because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.
questions.explanation: The speed question is less subjective because it focuses on a completed text input task and compares interfaces on speed.

questions.question: Why can subjective feedback still fail to support a definitive conclusion for a clear question about which text-entry interface is faster?
options: Because text-entry speed is impossible to measure.
Because every user would naturally agree on the faster interface.
Because the two interfaces cannot be tested with a task.
Because users' responses can split.
questions.explanation: Even for a clear faster-interface question, subjective feedback may not support a definitive conclusion because user responses can split.

questions.question: How does an experiment collect objective data to determine which text-entry interface is faster?
options: By counting the number of features provided by each interface.
By having all users input the same text and comparing their logged characters per minute.
By asking each user which interface feels faster after use.
By letting users choose different texts and report their satisfaction.
questions.explanation: The experiment collects objective data by using the same input text for all users and comparing their logged speed values in characters per minute.

questions.question: Which characteristic makes a research question testable?
options: It supports objective data collection.
It asks whether an interface is good.
It depends on overall user preference.
It relies on subjective user interpretation.
questions.explanation: A testable research question allows a study to collect objective data and draw conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

questions.question: Why is a research question framed around whether an interface is good generally problematic?
options: It asks for objective text entry speed.
It compares two interfaces on one measurable variable.
It is too specific to test.
It uses an ambiguous generalized concept.
questions.explanation: Questions framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.

questions.question: Why may a testable question about whether one interface is faster than another not fully answer whether it is better?
options: Speed and overall quality are different concepts.
A faster interface must be better for all users.
Speed cannot be measured objectively in a study.
Faster and better mean the same thing in usability.
questions.explanation: A testable question about speed may answer one aspect, but faster and better are different concepts, so it may not answer the broader better question.

questions.question: How can a study address a broader untestable usability question while remaining scientifically testable?
options: By choosing one testable question and treating it as the whole answer.
By replacing testable questions with subjective ratings.
By asking a single generalized question about overall goodness.
By combining conclusions from multiple testable questions about different aspects.
questions.explanation: An empirical study can frame multiple testable questions covering different aspects and combine their conclusions to reach a conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question.

questions.question: What is an independent variable in an empirical usability experiment?
options: A set of values assigned to a factor in an experiment
A variable whose value depends on the levels of a factor
A variable whose values are assigned and controlled
A condition created when a factor is combined with its values
questions.explanation: An independent variable, also called a factor, is defined as a variable whose values are assigned and controlled.

questions.question: What are the levels of an independent variable?
options: The dependent variables that depend on the factor levels
The test conditions produced when factors are combined with values
The values assigned to the independent variable or factor
The independent variables assigned and controlled in the experiment
questions.explanation: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

questions.question: In a text-entry interface experiment, what do the levels of the interface factor define?
options: Two dependent variables, interface and text entry speed
Two test conditions, one for the course's design and one for MS Word
Two user characteristics used to choose experiment participants
Two research questions about text entry speed and overall usability
questions.explanation: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor's two levels create two test conditions.

questions.question: Why is text entry rate a dependent variable in the text-entry interface experiment?
options: Because its value depends on the interface levels
Because its values are assigned and controlled to create test conditions
Because it is a user characteristic measured in the study
Because it is combined with its levels to produce experiment conditions
questions.explanation: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; text entry rate depends on the interface levels.

questions.question: Empirical evaluation is best described as:
options: Measurement of hardware performance in a controlled laboratory
Observation in the real world of real users
Evaluation of a system using only design documents
Observation of simulated users in a virtual environment
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, empirical research, or usability research, means observation in the real world of real users.

questions.question: In an XR system development process, empirical evaluation is carried out:
options: Before implementation to compare different user groups
During system design to choose display hardware
At the end, when the system is fully implemented
After requirements have been gathered but before design
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability of the system.

questions.question: Which are the first two stages in the empirical research process?
options: Test condition selection and result interpretation
Requirement gathering and system design
Research question framing and variables
System implementation and optimization
questions.explanation: The empirical research process has four stages, with research question framing as the first stage and variables as the second stage.

questions.question: In empirical research, how is a broader untestable question addressed?
options: By testing a single untestable question until it becomes objective
By directly collecting subjective feedback about the untestable question
By framing multiple testable questions and combining their definite conclusions
By replacing the untestable question with a generalized concept
questions.explanation: Research question framing addresses broader generalizable untestable questions by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, and combining the resulting conclusions.

questions.question: In the variables stage, how do independent variables and dependent variables differ?
options: Independent variables, or factors, can take levels or values, while dependent variables depend on those factors and levels
Factors are the values that depend on levels, while levels are the variables being measured
Independent variables depend on factors and levels, while dependent variables take levels or values
Independent variables are measured as outcomes, while dependent variables are assigned and controlled
questions.explanation: In the variables stage, independent variables or factors can take levels or values, and dependent variables are variables whose values depend on those factors and levels.

Question framing stage
Data analysis stage
Code testing stage
items.reason: Question framing, variable determination, and data analysis are stages of an empirical study, while code testing is an earlier implementation stage that precedes empirical evaluation.

Usability study

items.reason: Empirical study, usability study, and empirical research are names for the empirical evaluation of a developed system, while prototype evaluation is a limited early check of prototypes.

Objective data

items.reason: Objective data, text entry speed, and characters per minute are objective measures of text entry, while subjective feedback is user opinion rather than an objectively logged measure.

questions.question: Why does empirical evaluation come after code testing in interactive system development, and why does code testing not complete the usability assessment?
questions.reference_answer: Empirical evaluation is a stage in interactive system development that evaluates the usability of a developed system with end users. Code testing produces an executable system, but it does not establish whether the system is usable. Usability is how good a system is from the user's point of view, so user-based evaluation is needed after code testing.

questions.question: Why are quick prototype evaluations insufficient for a final usability assessment, and what form does a conclusive assessment of an implemented system take?
questions.reference_answer: Quick prototype evaluations use a limited number of evaluators on prototypes, so they can identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about overall usability. A conclusive usability assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with more users. It is conducted through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

questions.question: Why is a question such as whether an interface is good weak for empirical research, and how can a study still reach a conclusion about that broader question?
questions.reference_answer: Asking whether an interface is good can produce divided subjective judgments, so no answer or conclusion can be drawn. Generalized concepts such as goodness are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions. To balance testability and generalization, an empirical study frames multiple testable questions covering different aspects, reaches reliable conclusions for them, and combines those conclusions to answer the broader untestable question.

questions.question: In a usability experiment comparing an XR text input interface with Microsoft Word on text entry speed, how are the independent variable, its levels, and the dependent variable related?
questions.reference_answer: The interface is the independent variable, also called a factor, and the values assigned to it are its levels. In the text-entry example, the interface levels, such as the course's design and Microsoft Word, create test conditions in which text entry speed is observed. The text entry rate is the dependent variable because it depends on those interface levels, and logging speed as characters per minute provides an objective comparison.
